messages.content: You “I’m sure you’ll come up with something Draconia” I grin at her. To hermoine “you should meet my mom some day, she’d love you”

Hermione's head snaps up. "You mean that? An actual correspondence — or visit?" She catches her tone, composes herself. "That would be. Yes. Very valuable."

"She'll interrogate you for three hours," you warn, "and it'll be the best conversation of your life."

"Threaten me with a good time," Hermione says.

Behind you, Draconia sniffs audibly. "How *touching*. Press, when you tire of charity cases—" she lifts her chin, "—I pay in kind. Real materials. Restricted archive access. Think about who you want in your corner."

"She's recruiting him," Draco mutters to no one, disgusted.
I laugh at draconias word “ray of sunshine, are you. Let’s meet in the library tonight. We can chat.” To hermoine I just wink

Draconia blinks — once — caught off-guard by how easily you folded her recruitment into a yes. "The library. Tonight. Eight o'clock." She recovers her imperiousness instantly. "Don't be late, and don't be drunk."

"I make no promises on either front."

"I *do*," Draco mutters, dragging his crew away, "attend the same library. Unfortunately."

As the Slytherins scatter, Fred loops an arm around your shoulder. "You just booked a working session with Draconia Malfoy and winked at Hermione Granger in the same minute. It's been *two days*, mate."
I show up to the library after having had only two glasses of wine. It’s around 8

The library at eight is hushed and lamplit. You find Draconia at a corner table fortified like a siege camp — stacked books, fresh parchment, a quill laid crosswise like a drawn wand.

She looks up, nostrils flaring faintly. "Two glasses. I can *smell* it. Sit down before I reconsider."

She slides a parchment toward you — dense, tight handwriting, a sketched gating diagram dominating the page.

"Your discharge wasted at least thirty percent. Here's where."
I review the work. “You’ve been busy”

"Since *two o'clock*, yes." Her tone dares you to be impressed and forbids you to enjoy it.

She taps the diagram. "Your vent path opens wide and lets the surplus scatter omnidirectionally. Elegant spectacle, wasteful engineering. Gate the release through a stepped aperture—" her quill stabs three points on the sketch, "—here, here, and here, and you redirect that loss into the cycle itself. My estimate: thirty percent recovered, possibly more."

She leans back, watching your face with sharp green eyes. "Well? Tell me I'm wrong. I'll enjoy that less than you think."
You “You’re right. I think you’re missing why I did it. *for* the spectacle” I grin at her

Draconia sets her quill down with deliberate slowness.

"The *spectacle*," she repeats, in the voice of someone cataloguing evidence for a trial. "You under-engineered a research demonstration — *on purpose* — for theatre."

Something twitches at the corner of her mouth. She kills it. "Accidental genius is still genius, I suppose."

She slides a second parchment across. "Now stop grinning and look at this. Stepped-aperture gating. If your metering sigils can interface with it, the recovered thirty percent feeds back into the recursion — your deliberately-failing rune lasts nearly twice as long before venting."

Her eyes lift to yours. "That's not a patch, Press. That's a fusion."
I lean back. I’m sitting next to her. “Still isn’t solving the bigger problem. How to control the recursive build with general casting”

"No," she agrees, no defeat in it — just the clean pleasure of a hard problem. "Doubling the runway isn't landing the plane."

She pulls fresh parchment, quill racing. "So think smaller. Recursion compounds when the return path exceeds the loop's *spend*. In your demonstration that was deliberate. In general casting, it's leakage — casters lose energy back into their own structure and never notice."

Her eyes narrow. "Meter it. Skim the return every cycle and discharge the skim continuously — quietly, invisibly. Not a vent. A *habit*."

She looks up. "Can your sigils run passively? Always on?"

The sigils converge on the junction, flaring red where the trigger meets the containment matrix. The flow pattern is jagged — surges, then starvation.

"Look at that," George breathes. "The power's lurching. Trigger fires, the charm gulps everything at once, and the containment just — chokes."

"So sometimes it faints you," Fred says, watching the glowing map, "and sometimes it starves and you sneeze. Eleven rebuilds and it was a *flow* problem the whole time?"

He turns to you, eyes bright. "Can you fix that? What would it take?"
I fish in my ropes for a fine craving knife. “Gimme a second” I get down on my knees in front of the bench and crave a rune into the box.  Very light, almost unnoticeable

You kneel, and the knife moves with practiced precision — a hairline sigil traced into the wooden base, so fine it would pass for grain. Feed, meter, stabilize, bound into a loop.

"Metering array," you murmur. "Doles the power out steady instead of letting the trigger gulp."

"Test it," George says immediately, grabbing a spare. Fred snatches the modified one first.

"I'll do it." He holds the box like a bomb disposal expert, glances at George — "If this works, I'm claiming seniority" — and thumbs the catch.

The charm fires clean: a soft *whump*, then silence.

Fred drops like a sack of flour.

For one horrified second the room is silent — then George bursts out laughing, doubled over against the shelf. "MARK FOUR! IT ACTUALLY WORKS!"

Fred comes to about four seconds later, blinking at the ceiling from the floor. "Clean faint," he says thickly. "Full production-quality faint. No sneeze, no stutter, nothing."

He rolls over and looks up at you with the expression of a man witnessing religion. "Seth. Seth. That took you what, ninety seconds?"

"One knife," George adds reverently.
